Image alternative text starts with a redundant phrase
Remove the redundant opening phrase from the alt text. Before: alt="photo of our team". After: alt="Our team at the 2025 company retreat".
Screen readers already announce images before reading alt text. Starting with phrases such as "photo of" makes the output repetitive.
Image alternative text is too long
Shorten the alt text to describe the essential purpose of the image. Move detailed descriptions into the surrounding text or a linked description page.
Long alt text makes screen reader navigation tedious. Alt text should convey meaning, not reproduce entire image descriptions.
Link text is a raw URL or filename
Replace the URL or filename with descriptive text that explains the link destination. Example: Download annual report 2024 (PDF).
Screen readers may read URLs character by character. Raw URLs and filenames often do not explain the link destination.
Link points to a document file — verify accessibility

This is a review item, not an automatic failure. Verify manually whether accessibility requirements are met. Ensure the linked document is accessible and the link text describes the document and includes the file type.
Documents linked from websites must also be accessible. Inaccessible PDFs and Office documents can exclude users with disabilities.
Document link does not mention file type
Add the file type to the link text. Example: Download our annual report (PDF).
Users need to know whether a link opens a file instead of a web page so they can prepare their assistive technology or document reader.
Image alternative text quality issue in media record
Edit the image record and improve the alternative text. Remove redundant phrases and keep the description concise.
Poor alternative text in a media reference affects every place where that image reference is rendered.
Add a visible label to the form field in the EXT:form editor. Every user input field must have a label to be accessible.
Form fields without labels cannot be identified by screen readers or other assistive technologies. This prevents users with disabilities from completing forms.
Form field uses placeholder text instead of a label
Add a visible label to the form field in the EXT:form editor. Do not rely on placeholder text as the only field identification.
Placeholder text disappears when users start typing and is not reliably announced by screen readers as a label.
Same link text points to different destinations
Use unique link text that describes each destination, or add context via aria-label or surrounding text.
Users who navigate by links need to understand where each link goes. Reusing the same text for different destinations can be confusing.
Header content element is configured as H1
This is a review item, not an automatic failure. Verify manually whether accessibility requirements are met. H1 is typically reserved for the main page heading.
A clear heading structure helps users understand the page outline. Multiple or misplaced H1 headings can make navigation harder.
Media content should be reviewed for captions or transcripts
This is a review item, not an automatic failure. Verify manually whether captions, transcripts or other required alternatives for time-based media are available.
Audio and video content may need captions, transcripts or audio descriptions so users with disabilities can access the information.
Personal data field is missing autocomplete attribute
Add the appropriate autocomplete attribute to personal information fields in EXT:form. Examples: email, given-name, tel.
Autocomplete helps users with cognitive disabilities, motor impairments and anyone using browser autofill.
Image is missing an alt attribute
Add descriptive alt text for meaningful images. For decorative images, use an empty alt attribute: alt="".
The rendered HTML is what assistive technologies consume. Meaningful images need text alternatives.
Add visible link text or an accessible label that describes the destination.
Links without accessible names cannot be understood by screen reader users.
Add visible button text or an accessible label such as aria-label.
Buttons need an accessible name so users understand the action before activating it.
Add a short title attribute that describes the iframe content.
Iframe titles help assistive technology users understand embedded content.
Form control has no accessible label
Add a visible label, aria-label, or valid aria-labelledby reference.
Users need labels to understand the purpose of form fields.
Remove the empty heading or add meaningful heading text.
Empty headings create confusing landmarks in screen reader heading navigation.
Ensure each id attribute is unique in the final HTML document.
Duplicate IDs can break labels, descriptions, scripting and assistive technology references.
Add th cells for data tables, or mark layout tables as presentation.
Table headers help users understand relationships between cells.
Add meaningful text to the table header cell or remove the empty header.
Empty th cells provide no useful structure for assistive technologies.
Add aria-hidden="true" for decorative SVGs, or add a title, aria-label, or valid aria-labelledby for meaningful SVG graphics.
Meaningful SVG graphics need an accessible name so their purpose can be understood.
Set the lang attribute on the html element according to the page language.
The lang attribute helps screen readers choose the correct pronunciation rules.
Add a meaningful title element for the page.
Page titles help users identify where they are and distinguish browser tabs.
Page may be missing a main landmark
This is a review item, not an automatic failure. Verify manually whether the page has a clear main landmark using main or role="main".
A main landmark helps keyboard and screen reader users jump directly to the primary content.

Start by adjusting foreground or background colors so visible text has sufficient contrast.
Touch targets are too small or too close together
Small or closely spaced targets can be difficult to activate for people with motor impairments or touch device users.
Increase the target size or spacing so interactive controls can be activated reliably.
Landmarks help assistive technology users understand and navigate the page structure.
Place page content inside appropriate landmark regions such as header, main, navigation and footer.
Repeated landmarks with the same name can make page navigation confusing for screen reader users.
Give repeated landmarks unique accessible names or simplify the landmark structure.
Moving content can distract users and may be difficult to read or pause.
Remove marquee content or provide controls to pause, stop or hide moving content.
Image alt text looks like a filename
File names rarely describe the meaning of an image for people using screen readers.
Replace the filename-like alt text with a meaningful description of the image.
Generic link text makes it hard to understand links out of context.
Use link text that describes the destination or action.
Duplicate IDs can break label associations, ARIA references, links and in-page navigation.
Make every id attribute unique on the page and update all labels, links and ARIA references that point to the changed ID.
People using assistive technology need a programmatic label to understand the purpose of each form field.

Associate the form control with a visible label. When a visible label cannot be used, provide a clear accessible name with aria-label or aria-labelledby. A title attribute is accepted only as a last programmatic fallback.
Image alternative text is too long
Overly long alternative text can make content harder to understand and navigate.
Keep alternative text concise and describe only the information needed in context.
Image alternative text contains redundant wording
Phrases such as “image of” repeat information already announced by assistive technology.
Remove redundant phrases and describe the image purpose directly.
Identical link text points to different destinations
Identical link text for different destinations can be confusing out of context.
Use link text that distinguishes the destination or purpose of each link.
Link text is a URL or filename
Raw URLs and filenames often do not explain the link purpose clearly.
Replace the URL or filename with descriptive link text.
Users benefit from knowing that a link opens or downloads a document.
Make the document type and purpose clear in the link text or nearby context.
Document link does not identify the file type
Users may not know that a link opens a document or what format to expect.
Add a short file type or document notice to the link text or adjacent text.
Low-quality alternative text may not communicate the image purpose.
Replace generic, redundant or filename-like text with a concise meaningful description.
A clear label helps users understand what information a form field requires.
Add a visible label and associate it with the form control.
Placeholder is used instead of a label
Placeholder text disappears during input and is not a reliable replacement for a label.
Add a persistent visible label and keep placeholder text only as optional guidance.
Personal data field is missing autocomplete information
Autocomplete can reduce input effort and support users with cognitive or motor impairments.
Add the appropriate autocomplete token for the requested personal information.
Media content may need a transcript
A transcript provides access to spoken information for people who cannot hear the audio.
Provide a transcript or equivalent text alternative when the media contains meaningful audio.
Content element uses an H1 heading
Multiple or misplaced H1 headings can make the page structure harder to understand.
Use the heading level that matches the content hierarchy and reserve the page H1 for the main page topic.
Empty headings create confusing stops in screen reader heading navigation and make the page structure harder to understand.
Remove the empty heading element or add meaningful heading text that describes the following section.
A single main landmark helps screen reader and keyboard users find the primary page content quickly.
Keep exactly one main landmark on the page, using the main element or role="main".
A clear H1 helps people understand the page topic and navigate the content structure.
Add one meaningful H1 heading that describes the main purpose of the page.
Headings in a logical order help people understand the page outline and move through it quickly.
Use heading levels in a logical nested order and do not skip levels for visual styling; change the look with CSS instead.
The page title is the first context people get when they switch tabs, use bookmarks or navigate with assistive technology.
Give every page a concise, unique and descriptive title. In TYPO3 this is usually the page title or the SEO title of the page.
The page language lets screen readers use the correct pronunciation and helps browsers process the content correctly.
Set a valid lang attribute on the html element, for example lang="de". This is usually part of the site language or template configuration.
Assistive technologies may ignore invalid ARIA attributes or announce misleading information.
Remove invalid ARIA attributes or replace them with valid attributes supported for the element and its role.
Use ARIA attributes only where allowed
ARIA attributes on roles or elements that do not support them create confusing or incorrect semantics.
Use only ARIA attributes that are allowed for the role of the element, or change the markup to the correct semantic element.
Some ARIA roles need specific attributes so assistive technologies can understand the state or relationship of a widget.
Add the attributes the role requires, or replace the custom widget with native HTML where possible.
Some ARIA roles need specific child roles so assistive technologies can interpret complex widgets correctly.
Add the required child elements or roles, or use native HTML elements that already provide the correct structure.
Add the required ARIA parent role
Some ARIA roles must be inside a specific parent role to be announced and navigated correctly.
Place the element inside the required parent role, or use native HTML structures that provide the correct parent-child relationship.
